23 A cathode-ray oscilloscope (CRO) is used to display a wave of frequency 5.0 kHz. The display is
shown.
1 cm
1 cm
What is the time-base setting of the CRO?
A
10 µs cm–1
B
100 µs cm–1
C
10 ms cm–1
D
100 ms cm–1

hints: Count how many complete sine cycles are shown across the $10\text{ cm}$ wide screen and find the horizontal length of one cycle in cm.
Convert the given frequency $5.0\text{ kHz}$ to period $T = 1/f$ in $\mu\text{s}$ to get the time for that one cycle.
Divide the time for one cycle by its length in cm to get the time-base in $\mu\text{s cm}^{-1}$.
walkthrough: Find the period from the frequency: $T = 1/f = 1/(5.0 \times 10^3\text{ Hz}) = 2.0 \times 10^{-4}\text{ s} = 200\text{ }\mu\text{s}$.
Use the 1 cm grid to measure one wave: successive peaks are $2\text{ cm}$ apart, so wavelength on screen is $2\text{ cm}$.
Check the total: the $10\text{ cm}$ wide display contains $10/2 = 5$ complete cycles.
Time for the whole trace is $5 \times T = 5 \times 200\text{ }\mu\text{s} = 1000\text{ }\mu\text{s}$.
Time-base = total time / total distance = $1000\text{ }\mu\text{s} / 10\text{ cm} = 100\text{ }\mu\text{s cm}^{-1}$.

A.explanation: This is ten times too small because one full cycle occupies $2\text{ cm}$, not $0.2\text{ cm}$.

B.explanation: Five cycles of period $200\text{ }\mu\text{s}$ fill $10\text{ cm}$, giving $100\text{ }\mu\text{s cm}^{-1}$.

C.explanation: This confuses milliseconds with microseconds when converting the $0.20\text{ ms}$ period.

D.explanation: This is 1000 times too large because the $5.0\text{ kHz}$ period is in microseconds, not milliseconds.
